nameStory: The double-crested cormorant gets its name from the distinctive paired tufts of feathers that sprout from either side of its head during breeding season. These twin 'crests' give the bird a somewhat punk-rock appearance, with black and white plumage creating striking contrast. Outside of breeding season, these fancy feather decorations disappear, but the name stuck!
description: The double-crested cormorant is a large, sleek water bird that looks like a cross between a goose and a snake. These skilled underwater hunters are entirely black with long, flexible necks and sharp, hooked bills perfect for catching fish. They measure about 28-35 inches long - roughly the size of a small goose - but with a much more streamlined, athletic build designed for diving and swimming.

idTips.label: Distinctive drying pose
idTips.description: Often seen perched with wings spread wide open in a heraldic pose, holding this position motionless for long periods to dry their non-waterproof feathers

idTips.label: Orange-yellow facial patch
idTips.description: Bright bare skin around the bill and throat that stands out like a colorful mask against the all-black plumage

idTips.label: Swimming behavior
idTips.description: Swims low in the water with only head and neck visible above surface, then disappears completely underwater for 20-30 seconds while hunting

idTips.label: Long snake-like neck
idTips.description: Extremely flexible neck that appears almost serpentine, especially noticeable when the bird is swimming or perched

idTips.label: All-black plumage
idTips.description: Entirely black feathers with a slight iridescent sheen that can show greenish highlights in bright sunlight

idTips.label: Hooked bill
idTips.description: Sharp, pointed bill with a distinctive downward curve at the tip, designed for gripping slippery fish

habitat: Double-crested cormorants thrive around New England's lakes, rivers, coastal bays, and harbors where fish are abundant. You'll spot them perched on docks, rocky outcrops, dead trees, or navigation markers near water, always close to good fishing spots. They prefer areas with clear water where they can see their prey while diving, from mountain lakes to busy harbors.

seasonality.spring: Migrants return in March and April, with breeding birds developing their distinctive double crests and showing increased activity around nesting colonies on islands and coastal areas.
seasonality.summer: Most active period with birds diving frequently for fish and young birds learning to hunt. Adults lose their breeding crests by mid-summer but remain highly visible.
seasonality.fall: Large flocks gather before migration, creating impressive roosting congregations on favorite perches. Best time to see multiple birds together.
seasonality.winter: Some birds remain year-round in ice-free coastal areas, though most migrate south. Winter birds lack crests and may appear slightly duller.

funFact: Cormorants are one of the few birds that must hang their wings out to dry like laundry because their feathers aren't waterproof - this 'design flaw' actually helps them dive deeper since they don't have air trapped in their plumage making them too buoyant!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with loons, but cormorants have that distinctive wing-spreading drying behavior that loons never do, plus cormorants perch upright on posts and rocks while loons almost never leave the water. Remember: if it's hanging its wings out to dry, it's definitely a cormorant!
contextualKnowledge: Double-crested cormorants were nearly extinct in New England by the 1960s due to DDT poisoning, but have made such a remarkable comeback that they're now sometimes considered overabundant by fishermen and harbor managers. Their recovery is one of conservation's great success stories, though it sometimes creates new management challenges.
compareHints: In New England, the double-crested cormorant is the only cormorant species you're likely to encounter regularly, making identification straightforward. The similar Neotropic cormorant is much smaller and rarely ventures this far north. Great cormorants do visit New England coasts in winter but are noticeably larger with white throat patches and different facial coloring.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its close relative the Double-crested Cormorant, the Neotropic is significantly smaller and more slender, lacking the distinctive 'crests' that Double-crested sometimes show during breeding season.
